\title{Eleven Per Cent of a Statute Book:\\
The Enacted Law and the Applied Law in \nJudgments{} Judgments}

\begin{abstract}
\noindent
Empirical work on legislation measures what states enact. Empirical work on
courts measures what judges decide. The two are rarely joined, because doing
so needs both corpora for one jurisdiction at article level, and those do not
usually exist together. This article joins them for Saudi Arabia:
\nRegistryArticles{} articles across \nInstruments{} instruments, and
\nJudgments{} judgments in full text, published by the Ministry of Justice
through an open interface. \nCitations{} statutory citations are extracted
from the judgments and matched to the instruments, \nUnmatchedShare{} per cent
failing to match. Three findings follow. First, the applied law is a small
fraction of the enacted law: \nArticlesCited{} articles are cited at least
once, \nArticlesCitedShare{} per cent of the statute book, and
\nInstrumentsNever{} of \nInstruments{} instruments are never cited at all.
Second, what is applied is overwhelmingly procedural --- \nProceduralShare{}
per cent of citations --- and the single most-cited provision, cited
\nTopArticleCitations{} times, is the article stating which disputes the court
may hear at all. Third, and against the obvious explanation, the narrowing is
not imposed by the parties. Separating each judgment at its own headings, the
court cites procedure at \nReasoningProcedural{} per cent in its reasoning
against \nRecitalProcedural{} per cent in the statement of the case, and draws
on \nReasoningInstruments{} instruments where the statement of the case draws
on \nRecitalInstruments{}. The statement of the case is not the bar's voice
either --- at least \nRecitalByCourtShare{} per cent of its citations sit in a
sentence whose actor is the court, narrating a step it took --- and that
cuts the same way, because those citations are \nRecitalCourtProcedural{} per
cent procedural against \nRecitalOtherProcedural{} per cent for the rest. What
is put to the court is markedly less procedural than what the court answers
with. A fourth result is a null: amendment activity predicts neither citation
nor its absence. The enacted and the applied appear
to run in parallel rather than in dialogue.
\end{abstract}

\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} empirical legal studies; legislation; judicial
citation; legal informatics; open government data; Saudi Arabia
